## 1. FACT//DUEL — the 1v1 knowledge duel, rebuilt as a daily habit

**Kicker:** SEED ROUND — SEPTEMBER 2026  
**Kind:** title

**Subtitle:** A 1v1 sports-and-science knowledge duel, built as a daily habit before it is built as a business.

### Body

- A 3-4 minute head-to-head duel on sports and science, wrapped in a loop designed to bring you back tomorrow.

- Zero users outside a private playtest. Zero revenue. Stated here so it is never a discovery later.
- Raising $1.2M for 18 months to buy one thing: the retention data this deck does not have.

## 3. It did not die of distribution. It died of monetisation and long-tail retention.

**Kicker:** THE GRAVEYARD  
**Kind:** chart

### Body

- Trivia Royale: 2.5M downloads in about three weeks on a budget under $500,000 — blended under $0.20 per download.
- 45% day-one iOS retention, around 30 minutes of use a day. Closed eight months after launch; all 16 staff let go.
- HQ Trivia: 2.38M peak concurrent (28 Mar 2018), then 67,000 installs in Jan 2020 — 3.35% of its Feb 2018 rate.
- QuizUp: about $32.4M of equity raised; sold to Glu in 2016 for $7.5M of cancelled notes, booked at $3.2M fair value.
- Free installs and elite D1 were necessary and demonstrably not sufficient. Nobody solved day 30 or the dollar.

### Chart

`charts/graveyard.png` — see `scripts/investor-charts.py`.

### Sources

- [TechCrunch — Trivia Royale, 2.5M downloads in 3 weeks](https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/10/how-thor-fridrikssons-trivia-royale-earned-2-5m-downloads-in-3-weeks/)
- [SEC Form D — Teatime Games (Trivia Royale)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1717682/000171768218000001/primary_doc.xml)
- [TechCrunch — HQ Trivia shuts down](https://techcrunch.com/2020/02/14/hq-trivia-shuts-down/)
- [SEC Form D — HQ Trivia](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1734125/000173412518000001/xslFormDX01/primary_doc.xml)
- [SEC 10-K — Glu Mobile FY2016 (QuizUp mark)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1366246/000155837017001621/gluu-20161231x10k.htm)

### Speaker notes

This is the slide that decides whether an investor trusts the rest of the deck. Trivia Royale is the cleanest natural experiment in the category: it was built by QuizUp's own founder, it acquired 2.5M users at effectively zero cost, it posted 45% D1 — roughly the 90th percentile of all mobile games — and it was gone in eight months because revenue was insufficient and funding talks collapsed. Two caveats to state: the sub-$0.20 figure is blended cost per download including organic and viral, not a paid CPI, and the 45% D1 is company-reported to TechCrunch, not audited. Glu's $3.2M fair-value mark on QuizUp is the honest ceiling anyone should attach to a large unmonetised trivia audience. The takeaway line to say out loud: any pitch in this category that leads with 'we will go viral' is arguing the case that was already settled and ignoring the case that killed everyone. If asked what we would do differently, do not answer with features — answer with slide 4.

## 4. So the bet is sequencing: build the habit loop first, prove retention, then monetise.

**Kicker:** THE SOLUTION  
**Kind:** statement

### Body

- A duel is a 3-4 minute unit. The median mobile game session is 3.1-3.5 minutes; North America's is 3.64.
- Around the duel: XP and levels, day streaks with shields, three daily quests, achievements, a rank, gems, cosmetics.
- Solo expeditions and a curated calendar of real events carry the days when nobody wants a live opponent.
- Nothing in the product monetises today. That is deliberate, and it is the opposite of how this category usually fails.
- The order is the product decision. Retention is the gate; monetisation is downstream of a number we do not yet have.

### Screenshots

- `desktop-arena.png` — Choosing a format and an opponent. Every bot is labelled BOT before you play.
- `phone-arena.png` — The same choice on a phone.

### Sources

- [GameAnalytics — 2026 Mobile & PC Gaming Benchmarks](https://www.gameanalytics.com/reports/2026-mobile-pc-gaming-benchmarks)
- FACT//DUEL internal: public/product/investor/numbers.md §3.2 and §4.4

### Speaker notes

The session-length line is a design argument, not a traction claim, and must be framed that way: GameAnalytics' 2026 benchmark set (16,000+ games, nine regions, iOS and Android, CY2025) puts the median session at 3.1-3.5 minutes and North America at 3.64 minutes across 4.23 sessions a day. A duel is that unit by construction, which is why the duel and not the quiz-show format is the atom here. The long-tail apparatus — streaks, quests, achievements, a ladder, cosmetics — is the part every dead competitor either skipped or bolted on late. Be explicit that we are copying a known-good loop rather than inventing one; the honest claim is sequencing discipline, not novelty. Do not claim retention benefits from these mechanics: we have not measured any, and slide 9 says so.

## 5. The loop is shipped and playable. The measurement layer is the thing that is not.

**Kicker:** PRODUCT — THE DAILY LOOP  
**Kind:** product

### Body

- Home is the whole loop on one screen: level and XP, day streak, gems, rank, the day's quests, one-tap duel.
- The duel itself: fixed answer order, a reveal marker, an atomic answer write, and an inspectable round receipt.
- The practice opponent is labelled BOT and its planner never receives the question, the answer key or your response.
- Progression lives in IndexedDB on the device. There are no accounts and none of it reaches a server.
- That is the honest boundary of this build: we can ship the loop; we cannot yet measure whether it holds.

## 6. A calendar of real sports and science events gives the app a reason to exist on a Tuesday.

**Kicker:** PRODUCT — THE RETENTION SURFACE  
**Kind:** product

### Body

- Monthly limited-time modes open on real fixtures and announcements, then close when the window closes.
- Solo expeditions are short untimed routes with a Steady-or-Bold risk choice locked in before each answer.
- The calendar is static and hand-verified, with its verification date shown in the UI. No live feed, no scores API.
- This is the surface for the days nobody wants a live opponent — precisely the days the graveyard lost.
- The bank is 54 sourced questions today. Growing it is a funded milestone on slide 14, not a claim on this slide.

### Screenshots

- `desktop-journeys.png` — Expeditions: short untimed routes, a Steady-or-Bold choice, a stamp for finishing one.
- `phone-journeys.png` — Expeditions on a phone.

### Sources

- FACT//DUEL internal: public/product/investor/numbers.md — status paragraph and §5.15 (company disclosure)

### Speaker notes

The strategic point of this slide is that the thing that killed the category is the empty day, and a static curated calendar is a cheap, low-risk answer to it that needs no rights deal, no live data vendor and no scores licence. Be precise about what is not here: there is no live feed, no results service and no partnership with any league, broadcaster or rights holder — none is claimed anywhere in this deck. State 54 plainly rather than saying 'a growing bank'; a soft label here is the kind of ambiguity DocSend found invites 80% more scrutiny. The honest framing of content is that it is an operating cost with a known rate, which is why it appears as a line in the use of funds rather than as a feature.

## 7. $1.69bn – $2.83bn, counted bottom-up from people we can name.

**Kicker:** MARKET  
**Kind:** chart

### Body

- 216.8M US adults use a phone as a second screen during live sport, 2026 (EMARKETER estimate).
- 216.8M x $7.80-$13.07 revenue per active user per year = $1.69bn - $2.83bn.
- Both ends of that band are measured: Duolingo's FY2025 filing and MAG Interactive's interim report.

### Chart

`charts/tam-sam-som.png` — see `scripts/investor-charts.py`.

### Sources

- [EMARKETER — second-screen engagement during live sport](https://www.emarketer.com/content/second-screen-engagement-during-live-sports)
- [SEC — Duolingo FY2025 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026012246/q4fy25duolingo12-31x25shar.htm)
- [MAG Interactive — Q3 2025/26 interim report](https://storage.mfn.se/8d863483-ccc8-4f02-b0c5-d37d899b23e8/mag-interim-report-eng-2025-26-q3.pdf)
- [FSGA / Angus Reid 2026 — participation research](https://members.thefsga.org/news/Details/new-fsga-research-details-growing-role-of-ai-prediction-markets-in-fantasy-sports-and-sports-betting-341850)
- [Paul Graham — How to convince investors](https://paulgraham.com/convince.html)
- [a16z — 16 More Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-more-startup-metrics/)

### Speaker notes

This slide gets 29 seconds — third-least-read in the deck — so it carries one number and one arithmetic line and nothing else. Everything below lives in the appendix and in the answers. Method: Paul Graham's definition used literally, x customers x $y per year, with no penetration percentage anywhere in TAM or SAM, which is exactly a16z's toothbrush failure case avoided. The ARPU band is derived, not assumed: Duolingo $1,037.6M FY2025 revenue / 133.1M MAU = $7.80; MAG Interactive $21.563M of nine-month net sales / 2.2M MAU, annualised, = $13.07. MAG's figure is group-level across its whole portfolio, not QuizDuel standalone. SAM is the 90.3M North American adults who did fantasy sports or sports betting in the past year (FSGA 2026), giving $704M-$1.18bn — a bloc where 66% of 13-20-year-old season-long players update lineups daily at a $100 median annual spend. SOM is 0.14%-0.23% of SAM, and it is a chosen target with zero company data behind it, not a projection. We deliberately exclude Europe, Latin America and every science-audience bloc (followers and visits are not people, and they overlap the sports blocs), which makes the number smaller — say so, it is a credibility asset. If pushed on the global number, TAM-B of $9.49-15.90bn is in the appendix with the reason it is directional only: it applies US ARPU to a South Asian population, and Newzoo's own regional split contradicts that. One line worth saying: two paid research firms size game-based learning 3.93x apart for the identical year, so no vendor top-down number can discipline this plan.

## 10. We copy the habit subscription, not trivia IAP — and here is the cross-check that keeps us honest.

**Kicker:** BUSINESS MODEL  
**Kind:** chart

### Body

- Trivia IAP is the dead end: the top three true trivia apps on US iOS grossed $102.5K/week — $5.33M/yr, pre-Apple cut.
- Habit subscriptions are not: Duolingo $1,037.6M FY2025 at 9.03% MAU-to-paid; Kahoot $146.0M FY2022 at 95% margin.
- Our cross-check at base-case Year-3 scale (P): 105,900 MAU x 9.03% = 9,563 subs x $43.99 = $420,666.
- The install-economics route gives $1,630,517 (P) at the same scale — 3.88x more. So we present $0.4M - $1.6M (P).
- $43.99 is Sporcle's individual annual price. 9.03% is Duolingo's filed conversion. Neither is our number yet.

### Chart

`charts/where-money-is.png` — see `scripts/investor-charts.py`.

### Sources

- [Sensor Tower — Q2 2025 US iOS trivia revenue (est.)](https://sensortower.com/blog/2025-q2-ios-top-5-trivia%20games-revenue-us-604118ed241bc16eb8b8453a)
- [SEC — Duolingo Q2 FY2026 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026053299/q2fy26duolingo6-30x26share.htm)
- [SEC — Duolingo FY2025 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026012246/q4fy25duolingo12-31x25shar.htm)
- [Kahoot! — Q4 2022 quarterly report](https://kahoot.com/files/2023/02/4Q22_Kahoot_quarterly_report.pdf)
- [Sporcle — Orange membership pricing](https://www.sporcle.com/memberships/)
- [AppsFlyer — State of App Monetization 2026](https://www.appsflyer.com/resources/reports/app-marketing-monetization-report/)
- [GameAnalytics — 2026 Mobile & PC Gaming Benchmarks](https://www.gameanalytics.com/reports/2026-mobile-pc-gaming-benchmarks)

### Speaker notes

This is the longest-dwell slide in a seed deck at 64 seconds, so it is the densest page here and the one to rehearse hardest. The argument in one breath: the category does monetise, just not as consumer trivia IAP. Sensor Tower's Q2 2025 US iOS estimates put Kahoot at a $38.5K/week peak falling to $28.2K, Trivia Crack Premium at about $33K and GeoGuessr at $31K falling to $28.7K — $102.5K a week combined, $5.33M a year gross before Apple's 15-30% cut, and these are modelled estimates rather than audited revenue. Against that, Kahoot collected $146.0M in FY2022 at a 95% gross margin through subscriptions and Duolingo collects over a billion dollars a year from a streak-and-quest loop that is mechanically the same shape as ours. The cross-check is the point of the slide and it argues against us: at base-case Year-3 MAU of 105,900, a Duolingo-rate subscription at Sporcle's price yields $420,666, while our install-economics model yields $1,630,517 — a 3.88x divergence, which is why the honest Year-3 band is $0.4M-$1.6M and not $1.6M. In the conservative case the two routes land within 8% of each other, which is the reason to trust the conservative case and distrust the base case. Two ceilings to state before being asked: base-case revenue per MAU of $15.40/yr already exceeds both real anchors (MAG $13.07, Duolingo $7.80), and break-even blended cost per install is $1.36 in the base case against Trivia Royale's sourced sub-$0.20 — necessary, and demonstrably not sufficient. We have no verified CAC or genre ARPDAU benchmark and we will not quote one. All scenario figures are (P): plans built on third-party benchmarks, with zero company data behind them.

### Speaker notes

Competition gets 34 seconds, so the table has to do the work and the bullets only frame it. Putting our own row in with zeroes is deliberate: it is the row an investor would otherwise add themselves, and adding it first is worth more than the space it costs. Caveats: Trivia Crack's weekly figure is a Sensor Tower model, not disclosed revenue; MAG's MAU and net sales are group-level across its whole portfolio; Kahoot has published no audited consolidated group figures since delisting on 23 Jan 2024, so FY2022 is the last comparable full year (the parent-only Norwegian statutory accounts showing USD 112.824M for FY2025 are not group results and must not be compared like-for-like); and Wayground's frequently-cited ~$300M valuation appears in no primary source and is deliberately absent from this table. Skillz's FY2021-to-FY2025 collapse is the single most useful adjacent data point in the deck: $380.2M to $104.5M of revenue, 513,000 to 141,000 paying MAU, with monthly ARPPU essentially flat at about $62 throughout.

## 12. The risks that emptied this category are the first two on this list, and they set the milestones.

**Kicker:** RISKS  
**Kind:** bullets

### Body

- Long-tail retention. Trivia Royale had 45% D1 and died in eight months. Median D30 in this category is 0.68-0.79%.
- Opponent integrity. Skillz won $42.9M against AviaGames over bots run against paying humans in cash games.
- Benchmark transfer. Every retention, session and conversion figure here is measured on app-store installs, not web.
- Content depth. 54 questions is a demo bank. Production capacity is a funded line item, not an assumption.
- Model honesty. Our base case implicitly out-monetises a Duolingo-rate subscription by 3.88x. We flag it, not hide it.

### Sources

- [TechCrunch — Trivia Royale, 2.5M downloads in 3 weeks](https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/10/how-thor-fridrikssons-trivia-royale-earned-2-5m-downloads-in-3-weeks/)
- [GameAnalytics — 2026 Mobile & PC Gaming Benchmarks](https://www.gameanalytics.com/reports/2026-mobile-pc-gaming-benchmarks)
- [SEC 10-K — Skillz FY2023 (Skillz v. AviaGames)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1801661/000180166124000100/sklz-20231231.htm)
- [AppsFlyer — State of App Monetization 2026](https://www.appsflyer.com/resources/reports/app-marketing-monetization-report/)
- [SEC — Duolingo Q2 FY2026 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026053299/q2fy26duolingo6-30x26share.htm)

### Speaker notes

Each risk has a named response rather than a reassurance. Long-tail retention: the structural fact is that at a median D30 of 0.68-0.79% a game's MAU is almost entirely the current month's new installs — in our own base case the retained resident base is 5,900 of 105,900 MAU, 5.6% — so retention is not a metric in this category, it is the business, and that is why the entire raise is pointed at it. Opponent integrity: the AviaGames trial evidence described bots named 'Cucumbers' and 'Guides' run against paying humans, and the $42.9M willful-infringement verdict landed on 9 Feb 2024; in a 1v1 product this is a legal and existential issue rather than a feature, which is why our practice bot is labelled BOT in the UI, its planner never receives a question, answer key or human response, and all round plans are fixed and persisted before play. Benchmark transfer is the largest methodological risk in the whole model and is stated rather than buried: we have no verified benchmark for web-first game retention, web-first acquisition cost or web-first payer conversion, and the milestone-one cohort is what replaces the assumption with data. Content depth and model honesty are the two we control. If an investor adds a risk we have not listed, that is a good outcome — write it down and answer it in the follow-up, not on the spot.

## 14. $1.2M for 18 months, to buy the one number this deck does not have.

**Kicker:** THE ASK  
**Kind:** ask

### Body

- 4 engineers x $15,000/month x 18 months = $1,080,000. Raising about $1.2M, inside YC's $500k-$1.5M band.
- At Carta's Q3 2025 median seed pre-money of $16.0M: $1.2M into $17.2M post = 6.98% dilution.
- At a $24.0M post-money, Carta's Q4 2025 all-time high: 5.00%. Both under YC's 'as little as 10% is wonderful'.
- It buys: accounts and instrumentation, a published D1/D7/D30 cohort of 1,000+, and a larger question bank.
- Plus an opponent-integrity answer and one validated monetisation route. Then we come back with data, not benchmarks.

### Sources

- [Y Combinator — A guide to seed fundraising](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/4A-a-guide-to-seed-fundraising)

### Speaker notes

The ask uses YC's structure — N months x team x cost = $X, with dilution against published medians — and the arithmetic is shown so it can be checked in the 32 seconds this slide gets. The caveat to volunteer rather than defend: YC's $15,000 per engineer per month and its $500k-$1.5M band are undated editorial rules of thumb, not measured or inflation-indexed 2026 figures, and are very likely understated today; we use the structure and expect to substitute a current, defensible cost base when the team on slide 13 is real. Carta's $16.0M is the Q3 2025 median seed pre-money, up 14% YoY, in a quarter with about 17% down rounds; the $24.0M post-money is Carta's Q4 2025 all-time high across all sectors, with no consumer split published, so it is an upper anchor rather than a comparable. Base-case Year-1 revenue of $101,907 (P) is immaterial to runway and should be described that way — the raise buys 18 months to produce the retention data we do not have, which is the entire thesis of the round. No detailed financial model belongs in this conversation: a16z, YC and CRV all put three-to-five-year projections in the appendix or the data room, and ours is in appendix slide 16 where it can be interrogated rather than performed.

## 15. Appendix A — the ~1,000x gap between the category's claimed size and its observed revenue.

**Kicker:** APPENDIX — MARKET STRUCTURE  
**Kind:** appendix

### Body

- Top-down vendors size the nearest categories at $3.0bn (second-screen sports apps) to $8.09bn (fan engagement).
- Observed: the top three true trivia apps on US iOS grossed $5.33M/yr. The gap is roughly three orders of magnitude.
- Thesis reading: the category is structurally under-monetised — 267,939,837 Trivia Crack installs, product abandoned.
- Risk reading: trivia audiences do not pay and this is the ceiling. HQ, QuizUp and Trivia Royale all died with audiences.
- The reconciliation is slide 10: the category monetises through habit subscriptions, not consumer trivia IAP.

Present both readings and let the investor pick; a deck that only presents the thesis reading of a 1,000x gap has not understood it. The vendor disagreement is itself evidence: IMARC sizes game-based learning at $24.5bn for the same year MarketsandMarkets sizes it at $6.23bn, a 3.93x spread, and market.us sizes fan engagement at 2.00x The Business Research Company's figure. When two paid research firms differ by four times on the same market in the same year, neither number can discipline a business plan, which is the empirical case for the bottom-up construction on slide 7. Note also that our own TAM-A of $1.69-2.83bn sits below the top-down range, because we count only US second-screen adults at observed per-user revenue while the vendors count sponsorship, ticketing, merchandising and B2B platform spend we will never touch. All Sensor Tower figures are modelled estimates of gross consumer spend, before Apple's 15-30% cut.

This page exists only because someone asked for it. a16z lists detailed three-to-five-year projections among the things not to include, wants 12-18 month milestones instead, and its anchoring rule cannot even be satisfied here because we have no historical data to anchor to — which is itself the most honest sentence on the page. Inputs, all third-party: D30 retention of 0.68% / 1.18% / 1.70% (global median low, North American median, global P75 from GameAnalytics); install-to-payer of 5.08% / 11.14% / 18.46% (AppsFlyer NA repeat payer, NA one-time payer, and a derived $1.34/$7.26 ratio used only as an optimistic ceiling and labelled derived); ARPPU held at AppsFlyer's casual D90 $7.26 in all three; ad revenue per install $0.00 in the conservative case because we are a web app with no mediation stack today. Monthly churn of the retained base is fixed at 20% across all scenarios — an unsourced modelling assumption, held constant so it cannot flatter any scenario. Three stress tests all point the same way: the conservative case is genuinely conservative, and the base case is not. Base-case revenue per MAU of $15.40 exceeds both real anchors (MAG $13.07, Duolingo $7.80), so any scenario that out-monetises Duolingo per active user is a ceiling and not a target. Per-MAU revenue also looks high partly because high churn makes annual installs about 11x steady-state MAU — throughput, not intensity.

Two flaws to disclose before anyone finds them. First, a nesting inconsistency: TAM-A is US-only at 216.8M while SAM includes Canada at 90.3M (82.8M US plus about 7.5M Canadian), so roughly 7.5M people sit in SAM but not TAM-A. It is immaterial and it is flagged rather than smoothed over. Second, TAM-B is in this deck only as an upper bound with its own refutation attached. Why SAM is genuinely addressable rather than merely large, both from FSGA 2026: 66% of 13-20-year-old season-long fantasy players update lineups daily, with an average starting age of 14 and a $100 median annual spend, and 51% of participants do both fantasy and betting, up from 49%. That is a daily-habit, already-spending, competitively-motivated audience — the behavioural profile a 1v1 duel is built for. Nielsen's '51% of people globally are fans of football' is deliberately not converted to a headcount because we have no verified population denominator for it; we use only its 62M US soccer fans and the ICC's 1bn+ cricket figure. Aggregator fan-base numbers circulating for other sports failed verification and are excluded.

### Speaker notes

Precision notes that matter if challenged. QuizUp's '20 million users' is a company statement from 19 May 2014 describing a six-month registration milestone, not a measured peak — we quote it as claimed, attributed and dated. HQ Trivia's decline figure is the comparison of 67,000 installs in January 2020 against roughly 2 million a month in February 2018, which is 3.35%; it relaunched on 29 Mar 2020, played its last game on 17 Nov 2022 and was delisted from stores on 5 Aug 2023. Trivia Royale's 45% D1 and sub-$500,000 budget are company statements to TechCrunch, not audited, and the sub-$0.20 per download is blended including organic and viral rather than a paid CPI. Skillz's monthly ARPPU was $61.75 in FY2021 (derived) and $61.70 in FY2025 (stated) — essentially flat while the paying base fell 73%, which is the cleanest available evidence that competitive-play users monetise well and churn hard.

- FACT//DUEL internal: public/product/investor/numbers.md §4.1-§4.3

### Speaker notes

This is §4.3 of numbers.md reproduced in full, so that anyone who wants to check the arithmetic can do it on the page instead of asking for a spreadsheet. Two things to say before they are asked. First, the only thing that changes between scenarios is three inputs — D30 retention, install-to-payer rate and install volume; the model itself is identical, ARPPU is held at AppsFlyer's casual D90 $7.26 in all three, and monthly churn of the retained base is held at 20% everywhere so it cannot flatter one case. Second, the install volumes are chosen assumptions with no company data behind them, which is why appendix H lists them as assumptions rather than inputs. Revenue per MAU rises across scenarios only because higher churn makes annual installs about 11x steady-state MAU — that is throughput, not better monetisation, and it is the reason the subscription cross-check on slide 10 exists.

## 22. Appendix H — every input, every assumption, and which of them has no source.

**Kicker:** APPENDIX — INPUTS AND ASSUMPTIONS  
**Kind:** table

### Body

- Two rows in this table are not sourced: monthly churn, and the install volumes. Both are labelled.
- The 18.46% payer rate is arithmetic on two published AppsFlyer figures, used only as a ceiling.
- Break-even blended cost per install: $0.37 / $1.36 / $1.89 (P). Trivia Royale's was under $0.20.
- Base-case revenue per MAU of $15.40 exceeds MAG's $13.07 and Duolingo's $7.80. A ceiling, not a target.

### Table

| Input | Conservative | Base | Optimistic | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D30 retention | 0.68% | 1.18% | 1.70% | GameAnalytics CY2025: global median low / NA median / global P75 |
| Install to payer | 5.08% | 11.14% | 18.46% | AppsFlyer: NA repeat payer / NA one-time payer / derived $1.34 / $7.26 |
| ARPPU (D90) | $7.26 | $7.26 | $7.26 | AppsFlyer casual games D90 ARPPU |
| Ad revenue per install | $0.00 | $0.55 | $0.55 | AppsFlyer casual D90 IAA ARPU; $0.00 assumes no mediation stack, which is today's state |
| Monthly churn of retained base | 20% | 20% | 20% | Assumption, unsourced. Held constant so it cannot flatter a scenario |
| Installs Y1 / Y2 / Y3 | 25K / 90K / 250K | 75K / 350K / 1.2M | 200K / 1.0M / 4.0M | Assumptions. No company data behind them |

### Sources

- [GameAnalytics — 2026 Mobile & PC Gaming Benchmarks](https://www.gameanalytics.com/reports/2026-mobile-pc-gaming-benchmarks)
- [AppsFlyer — State of App Monetization 2026](https://www.appsflyer.com/resources/reports/app-marketing-monetization-report/)
- [TechCrunch — Trivia Royale, 2.5M downloads in 3 weeks](https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/10/how-thor-fridrikssons-trivia-royale-earned-2-5m-downloads-in-3-weeks/)
- [SEC — Duolingo FY2025 shareholder letter](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1562088/000162828026012246/q4fy25duolingo12-31x25shar.htm)
- [MAG Interactive — Q3 2025/26 interim report](https://storage.mfn.se/8d863483-ccc8-4f02-b0c5-d37d899b23e8/mag-interim-report-eng-2025-26-q3.pdf)
- FACT//DUEL internal: public/product/investor/numbers.md §4.1-§4.3

### Speaker notes

The point of showing the inputs separately from the outputs is that an investor can replace any one of them and re-run the model without our help. Even the optimistic case assumes only median casual per-install monetisation — AppsFlyer's own $1.34 IAP plus $0.55 ad revenue — so all of the optimism sits in install volume and none of it in monetisation quality. The derived 18.46% payer rate is arithmetic on two published figures that may rest on different samples and windows, and it sits well above the 11.14% North American 30-day figure, which is why it is used only as a ceiling and labelled derived. The conservative case carries $0.00 of ad revenue because we are a web app with no mediation stack today. On break-even cost per install: Trivia Royale's sourced blended figure of under $0.20 is inside all three of ours, and that company still died with 2.5M downloads and 45% D1, so clearing break-even is necessary and demonstrably not sufficient.
